opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What excites me about masking is that it's a really clean way to ask what a network already knows, without changing what it knows.

When you fine-tune a pretrained model, you update the weights, so it's hard to tell whether a capability was there all along or whether you just taught it during fine-tuning. With masking, you freeze the weights and only learn which ones to keep or turn off. You can't add new information through the weight values themselves. So if a masked subnetwork does well on a task, that's fairly strong evidence the capability was latent in the original model and you just had to select it.

That connects to something I found surprising from the lottery ticket and supermask work: a randomly initialized network, with no weight training at all, can perform far above chance if you choose the right mask. That tells you selection is a surprisingly powerful operation. With a pretrained model, the question becomes how much useful structure is sitting there waiting to be uncovered, and how it's organized. Are there distinct subnetworks for different tasks? Do they overlap? Is knowledge localized or spread out?

There's also a practical side. Masks are cheap to store, essentially one bit per weight, so you could keep one shared model and swap in different masks for different tasks. And from an interpretability perspective, a mask gives you a concrete artifact you can analyze: which layers it prunes, which heads it keeps, how it differs across tasks. So masking works both as a tool for adapting models and as a probe for understanding what pretraining actually put in there.

r001.rationale: The response says masking freezes the pretrained weights and selects subnetworks, then asks how subnetworks for different tasks overlap and where knowledge is organized. This communicates using masks to identify subnetworks associated with learned capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What excites me about masking is that it flips the usual question. Normally when we study a pretrained network, we ask what happens if we train it further on some task. Masking asks something different: what's already in there, if you don't change a single weight?

The setup is simple. You take a network, maybe randomly initialized, maybe pretrained, and you freeze it completely. The only thing you're allowed to learn is a binary mask, which decides which weights stay and which get zeroed out. And the surprising thing is how far that gets you. With a random network, if it's wide enough, you can find a subnetwork that already does the task reasonably well, without any weight ever being updated. That was the "supermask" result that came out of the lottery ticket work, and it reframes training as partly a search problem rather than purely an optimization problem.

With pretrained models, it becomes a probing tool. If I can learn a mask that extracts a capability from a frozen model, that tells me the capability was latent in the weights already. It's much more conservative evidence than fine-tuning gives you, because fine-tuning can add new function. A mask can only subtract. So when it works, you've shown the model contained a circuit for that behavior, and when it fails, that's informative too.

I also just find it a clean lens on what pretraining is actually doing. A lot of the mystery is whether these models store general-purpose features or something more entangled. Masking lets you ask, concretely, how much of the network you need to keep, and whether the pieces you keep for one task overlap with the pieces you keep for another. That gives you a kind of map of the model that's hard to get any other way.

r001.rationale: The response explains that learning a mask on a frozen pretrained model can extract a capability already latent in its weights, identifying the subnetworks associated with a task or behavior.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that masking gives us a fairly direct way to ask what a pretrained model has already learned. You keep the weights fixed, remove parts of the network, and see what it can still do. If you find a mask that produces useful behavior, then you’ve exposed something that was already available in those weights, rather than learning it by updating them.

There’s a caveat, though: finding the mask is itself an optimization process, so it isn’t a completely neutral readout of the model. But that’s part of what makes it interesting. You can investigate how much comes from pretraining and how much comes from selecting the right subset of the network. That gives us another way to study where a model’s capabilities come from.

r001.rationale: The response says masking a frozen model can reveal useful behavior already available in its weights, but it does not clearly identify subnetworks as responsible for particular characteristics or learned features.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that masking gives us a fairly simple way to ask what a pretrained model has learned. You can hold the weights fixed, selectively mask parts of the model, and see which capabilities survive. That helps separate what’s already available in the pretrained representation from what you might otherwise learn through fine-tuning.

There’s also something really interesting about finding a small subnetwork that performs a task well. How much of that behavior comes from pretraining, and how much comes from the way we selected the mask? I think that makes masking both a useful probe and a reason to be careful about what we mean when we say a model “knows” something.

r001.rationale: The response says the weights remain fixed while parts are masked to see which capabilities survive, and describes finding a small subnetwork that performs a task. This communicates probing a frozen pretrained model by identifying subnetworks associated with learned capabilities.
